sentences.text: Kaikaifilu was an extinct mosasaurine reptile belonging to the family Mosasauridae and the subfamily Tylosaurinae that lived in Antarctica during the Late Cretaceous.
The genus name Kaikaifilu honors Coi Coi-Vilu, a reptilian ocean deity from Mapuche cosmology, while the type species is Kaikaifilu hervei.
The species name hervei honors Chilean geologist Francisco Hervé for his contributions to the geology of Chile and the Antarctic Peninsula.
This animal is distinguished by well-marked heterodont dentition, a rare trait among mosasaurs that is absent in other tylosaurines and shared by only one other known species, Eremiasaurus.

Four distinct tooth types are known: medium conical teeth without wear facets, medium conical teeth with wear facets, very large conical teeth without wear facets, and small blunt D-shaped teeth with soft enamel likely representing growing teeth.
The pterygoid bone in Kaikaifilu is pointed in the rostral direction, an unusual feature among mosasaurs.

Unlike its contemporary Moanasaurus, Kaikaifilu features a pre-orbital constriction of the rostrum, and it possesses a prominent crest on the upper margin of the eye orbit and another crest between the two nostrils.

The preserved skull parts of the Kaikaifilu holotype measure about 0.7 meters long, suggesting a total skull length of 1.1 to 1.2 meters, which exceeds that of contemporary mosasaurs like Taniwhasaurus antarcticus.
With a maximum estimated length of 10 meters, Kaikaifilu is the largest known mosasaur in the Southern Hemisphere and potentially one of the largest tylosaurines.
Fossil evidence indicates Kaikaifilu lived in Antarctic waters that may have been below freezing, with average deep-shelf temperatures around 6°C.
Unlike Taniwhasaurus, Kaikaifilu has a prominent crest on the upper margin of the eye orbit and another crest between the two nostrils.
The only known species was described in 2017 from an incomplete specimen found in the López de Bertodano Formation on Seymour Island, Antarctic Peninsula, by Otero et al. in 2016.

In January 2011, the Chilean Paleontological Expedition collected a large mosasaur skull, associated jaw fragments, a partial humerus, and nearly 30 isolated teeth from the upper layers of the formation.
The specimen, cataloged as SGO.PV.6509, was found in rocks dating to the late Maastrichtian, about 200 meters below the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary.
Kaikaifilu was an apex predator that shared its habitat with invertebrates, fish, plesiosaurs, and other mosasaurs, and due to its large size, it likely preyed on plesiosaurs from the formation.
Fish fossils in the López de Bertodano Formation are dominated by Enchodus and ichthyodectiformes, and Kaikaifilu lived alongside the aristonectine plesiosaur Aristonectes.
Phylogenetic analyses show that Kaikaifilu is closely related to Tylosaurus and Taniwhasaurus within the subfamily Tylosaurinae.

As of 2019, the classification of Kaikaifilu within the subfamily Tylosaurinae has been questioned by researchers, who suggest that certain observed characteristics contradict the definition of the group.

Kaikaifilu lived during the Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous in what is now northern Antarctica, specifically during the Upper Maastrichtian in the López de Bertodano Formation on Seymour Island, Antarctic Peninsula.
The waters where Kaikaifilu lived were located at about 65°S, with average deep-shelf temperatures around 6°C and surface temperatures that may have dropped below freezing.
Dating to the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event, Kaikaifilu is considered one of the last known mosasaurs.
